articles.article: The city of Port Meridian opened its first seawater desalination plant on Tuesday, three years late and forty percent over its original budget. The plant, built on the site of the decommissioned Harbor Point generating station, is designed to supply a fifth of the city's drinking water and to cut its draw on the shrinking Blue Fork aquifer by half within a decade. Officials cited pandemic-era supply chains and two redesigns of the intake screens, ordered to protect juvenile flounder, as the main sources of delay. The final cost of the project reached 412 million dollars, up from the 294 million approved by voters in the 2019 bond measure. At the ribbon cutting, plant director Amara Osei called the project a hedge the city could no longer afford to skip. Droughts are no longer the exception here, and this plant is what turning on the tap in 2040 looks like, she said. Critics, including the harbor fishing cooperative, argue the plant's brine discharge will raise salinity in the outer harbor, and have petitioned the state water board for quarterly monitoring. The plant begins continuous operation next month, after a six-week commissioning run at half capacity.

Researchers at Calloway University reported on Thursday that their 48-qubit processor ran an error-corrected calculation for eleven minutes, a duration roughly two hundred times longer than the group's previous record. The result, published in the journal Applied Quantum Letters, relied on a new cooling assembly and a lattice of spare qubits that take over from failing neighbors mid-computation. The machine spent the eleven minutes repeatedly factoring small numbers, work a laptop does instantly, but the point was endurance rather than speed. Every useful quantum program we know of needs hours of stable runtime, and until now nobody had minutes, said lead author Priya Raghunathan. The team estimates that reaching one hour of stable operation will require doubling the spare-qubit lattice, which the university's new fabrication line is expected to deliver within two years. Independent reviewers called the cooling assembly the more significant contribution, noting that three other laboratories have already requested its specifications. The university has filed two patents on the design and says the specifications will be released to academic groups without charge.

Twelve bakeries across the Elmwood district will begin operating as a single cooperative on the first of next month, pooling their flour purchasing, delivery routes and overnight staff under an agreement signed this week. The cooperative, named the Elmwood Ovens Guild, was organized over eighteen months by two shop owners who started comparing invoices at a neighborhood association meeting and found they were paying wholesale prices that differed by a third. Under the agreement, each bakery keeps its own name, recipes and storefront, while a jointly owned depot on Foundry Street handles purchasing and dispatches a shared fleet of four electric vans. The guild projects a fifteen percent drop in ingredient costs in its first year and has committed half of the savings to raising overnight bakers' wages. We spent a century competing over who gets up earliest, and it turns out the ovens were never the hard part, said co-founder Teodora Vasquez, who has run her family's shop for twenty-two years. The city's small business office, which helped draft the bylaws, says it has fielded inquiries from florists and fishmongers about copying the model. The guild's first joint purchase, forty tons of winter wheat flour, arrives at the depot next week.
